Each animal must also be documented and evaluated before authorities can determine its condition and appropriate placement.

Budensiek said the final number of animals remained uncertain while the operation continued. Authorities were also working through legal questions involving ownership and whether the resident would voluntarily surrender the animals.

The response was expected to continue as crews worked through the property and arranged shelter and care for the animals.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County man leads Martin County deputies on high-speed chase through Indiantown
cards.teaser: A Palm Beach County man led Martin County deputies on a high-speed chase through Indiantown after driving more than 100 mph on State Road 710.
cards.body:
Deputies spotted 33-year-old Markell Tillman driving aggressively at speeds exceeding 100 mph on State Road 710, forcing other vehicles off the roadway. When deputies attempted to stop him, Tillman fled. He weaved through traffic in an attempt to lose deputies before turning onto SW Martin Highway toward Palm City, where he continued to drive recklessly.

 Deputies spotted Tillman again traveling eastbound on Martin Highway near Allapattah Road. Deputies used stop sticks to disable his vehicle near I-95.

 Tillman then bailed out of the vehicle and attempted to flee on foot before deputies caught up with him and took him into custody. He was arrested on fleeing and eluding, aggravated fleeing with injury or damage, operating a vehicle exceeding the speed limit by 50 or more mph, driving while license suspended or revoked, obstruction without violence, and operating a vehicle at 100 or more mph.

 Tillman also had an out-of-county warrant at the time of his arrest. He was booked into the Martin County Jail.

cards.headline: Murray Middle School demolition begins after Hurricane Milton tornado damage
cards.teaser: Murray Middle School demolition is underway in Martin County, marking the start of a major reconstruction effort following tornado damage caused by Hurricane Milton.
cards.body:
Murray Middle School demolition is underway in Martin County, marking the start of a major reconstruction effort following tornado damage caused by Hurricane Milton. The project includes reconstruction of buildings destroyed in the tornadoes, along with a new administration building, media center, art lab, and a full overhaul of the parking lot. The demolition phase alone costs $3.3 million, though the total project cost has not been finalized.

 The project is being funded by local capital improvement, sales tax and Public Education Capital Outlay. Students who were displaced from the affected classrooms will continue learning in portable classrooms until construction is complete.

 Kirstie Gernaine, coordinator of public information and community relations for the Martin County School District, said Murray Middle School was already slated to get all of this construction work with a new admin area, a new media center and a brand new art lab. With Hurricane Milton and those tornadoes destroying the buildings in the back buildings 18, 10, and nine, the district was able to add these on.

 The school district said parents can be assured their students will be safe during construction. Barriers have already been placed around the work zone to keep students out. The district hopes to complete the renovations by December 2027.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County residents adjust diets as E. coli and cyclospora outbreaks spread
cards.teaser: Health officials confirmed five local cases of cyclospora since May, including two in St. Lucie County and one in Martin County, prompting residents to change what they eat and avoid.
cards.body:
Concerns over contaminated produce linked to E. coli and cyclospora outbreaks are prompting South Florida residents to reconsider their food choices, with some avoiding leafy greens entirely. The outbreaks have affected thousands nationwide and include lettuce connected to Taco Bell locations. Health officials have confirmed local cases stretching from the Palm Beaches to the Treasure Coast, including two cases in St. Lucie County.

 The Florida Department of Health reported five confirmed local cases of cyclospora since May. Two cases were reported in Palm Beach County, two in St. Lucie County, and one in Martin County. The contamination concerns have led families across the region to change their eating habits at restaurants, grocery stores, and fast-food chains.

 Dakota and Brynlee Rhodes, who were visiting Delray Beach with their mother Jenny, said they are trying to stay away from lettuce and stuff like that. Other families are similarly steering clear of leafy greens altogether as reports of contaminated produce continue to spread across the country. The widespread nature of the outbreaks has left many consumers uncertain about which products are safe to purchase and consume.

 Samantha Barone, a dietitian for the bariatric program at Delray Medical Center, offered guidance for consumers looking to maintain healthy diets while avoiding potentially contaminated produce. Barone recommends sticking to melon and things that have a harder skin that you can peel. She advises consumers to focus on produce with protective outer layers and to wash all fruits and vegetables thoroughly before eating them.

 For those seeking alternatives to leafy greens, Barone suggests that beans and nuts are safe options that still provide fiber and protein. She specifically recommends cleaning produce using a mixture of one part distilled white vinegar to three parts water. The outbreaks have highlighted the importance of proper food handling and preparation practices for consumers across South Florida.

cards.headline: E. coli and cyclospora outbreaks hit Treasure Coast, residents avoid lettuce and berries
cards.teaser: Two confirmed cases of cyclospora infections occurred in St. Lucie County and one in Martin County since May, part of nationwide E. coli and cyclospora outbreaks linked to contamin
cards.body:
Two confirmed cases of cyclospora infections occurred in St. Lucie County and one in Martin County since May, part of nationwide E. coli and cyclospora outbreaks linked to contaminated lettuce, according to the Florida Department of Health. Palm Beach County reported two additional cases. Thousands across the United States have been affected by the outbreaks, including lettuce connected to Taco Bell locations.

 Residents across South Florida are changing their diets in response to the health threat. Dakota and Brynlee Rhodes, visiting Delray Beach with their mother Jenny, said they are staying away from lettuce. Jenny Rhodes said she misses salads and berries but prefers being careful.

 George Lorenz said he heard about the outbreak and is avoiding contaminated foods while eating pizza in downtown West Palm Beach on Clematis Street with his father Brian. Hendriette Peckens in Boynton Beach bought two big bags of oranges, bread and apples instead of produce and planned to cook Alaskan salmon for dinner.

 Samantha Barone, a dietitian for the bariatric program at Delray Medical Center, said consumers should focus on produce with protective outer layers like melons, bananas and avocados. She said people should stick to melon and things with harder skin that can be peeled, but emphasized the importance of washing them before cutting and peeling. Barone recommended washing all fruits and vegetables thoroughly before eating them and said beans and nuts are safe alternatives that provide fiber and protein.

 She warned against bagged lettuce and recommended buying whole heads of lettuce and peeling away the outer layers. She also advised avoiding berries, especially raspberries, because they are difficult to clean properly. Brian Lorenz said he is not avoiding anything but is washing all food.

 Barone recommended cleaning produce using a one to three part mixture of distilled white vinegar and water, then soaking, massaging and cleaning off produce before cooking vegetables. The outbreaks stem from contaminated produce that can cause severe stomach illness and intense diarrhea. Barone emphasized that the outbreaks are not an excuse to abandon healthy eating, telling people not to say to heck with fruits and vegetables and hit the donuts. She said consumers still want to remain healthy despite the contamination concerns affecting produce typically considered healthier options.

cards.headline: Two Martin County brush fires contained, more expected this summer
cards.teaser: Martin County saw two brush fires this week, including one sparked by a lightning strike, both now fully contained and being monitored by the Florida Forest Service.
cards.body:
Two brush fires broke out in Martin County this week, including one ignited by a lightning strike, and both are now fully contained and under monitoring by the Florida Forest Service. Officials are warning that conditions favorable for brush fires will continue throughout the summer months as the region remains in peak fire season.

 David Grubitch, a mitigation specialist and spokesperson with the Florida Forest Service, said summertime heat is drying out fine dead fuels, making them highly receptive when lightning strikes occur. However, he emphasized that residents should not be alarmed by these conditions, as they are typical for this time of year. Grubitch explained that while rain often extinguishes fires immediately after they start, some fires can travel underground and resurface days later, making them more difficult to detect and contain.

 The Florida Forest Service is relying on public assistance to help monitor and respond to brush fires quickly. Grubitch stressed that residents play a crucial role in helping the department do its job effectively and urged people to never assume someone else has already reported a brush fire they spot. He emphasized the importance of immediate notification, saying that if residents see something, they should say something, as it can make all the difference in how quickly crews are able to get a fire under control. Quick reporting remains one of the most effective tools in preventing small fires from becoming larger, more dangerous blazes that threaten homes and natural areas.

 With summer conditions expected to continue creating favorable environments for brush fires, the Florida Forest Service will maintain its heightened monitoring and response efforts throughout the season. The department continues to track contained fires and remains prepared to respond to new incidents as they arise. Residents are encouraged to remain vigilant and report any signs of smoke or fire to local authorities immediately, regardless of whether they believe others may have already called it in. Officials stress that multiple reports of the same fire are preferable to a fire going unreported and potentially spreading out of control.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound couple seeks support as husband battles head and neck cancer
cards.teaser: Dave and Faren Motz of Hobe Sound are asking for community support as Dave battles head and neck cancer, facing nearly $20,000 in out-of-pocket costs for treatment.
cards.body:
A Hobe Sound couple is asking for community support as they navigate a cancer diagnosis. Dave and Faren Motz met in South Florida before moving to Maui, where they married and raised their family. Faren homeschooled all three of their children, and the family started a farm where they served children. Years later, the couple moved to Hobe Sound and purchased a property, but just months after settling in, Dave was diagnosed with head and neck cancer.

 As the couple searched for healthcare in Florida, AdventHealth in Celebration provided programs and grants that became a critical resource. Dave underwent nearly seven weeks of daily radiation treatments. The repeated visits to Orlando, biopsies, scans, and exams added up, costing the couple nearly $20,000 out of pocket.

 Their age and income kept them from qualifying for Medicare or Medicaid. Dave, a former firefighter who had long been the family's provider, now has an 85% chance of recovery according to doctors. Faren now works to support them both at Latitudes at the Jupiter Beach Resort, where those who want to show support can visit. Those who would like to contribute financially can donate to the family's GoFundMe at Standing with Dave Motz in his cancer battle.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County firefighter terminations questioned as police report contradicts hazing findings
hero.teaser: Three St. Lucie County firefighters were fired following an outside investigation into alleged hazing, but a Fort Pierce Police report and community members are challenging whether the punishment fits the case.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Fire Chief Jeff Lee announced over the weekend the termination of three senior St. Lucie County firefighters following an investigation into an alleged hazing incident reported to the department in March 2026. An investigative summary prepared by an outside law firm hired by the St. Lucie County Fire District concluded that senior personnel had modified a bug zapper to shock three apprentice firefighters while on duty in 2024. The investigation was launched after six videos surfaced that the report says appeared to show hazing, workplace violence or other misconduct. Three supervisors were fired, while two other firefighters were suspended. Chief Lee told WPTV the terminations were not based on this incident alone, pointing to four prior harassment complaints involving Station 1, including one that specifically named the three fired firefighters.

A Fort Pierce Police report obtained by WPTV reaches a very different conclusion. A Fort Pierce police officer wrote that after interviewing the three firefighters who were shocked, found there was no criminal matter behind the alleged hazing and that the videos showed coworkers entertaining each other. The report also states the acts were done by their own will, and that every person originally listed as a victim said they are not victims and did not want to continue the investigation. Retired Fire Captain Mike Jenkins, who served more than 30 years with the department, watched the videos and said he does not believe they show hazing. The St. Lucie County Chapter of the Professional Fire Fighters & Paramedics Union is demanding arbitration on behalf of the five firefighters, with President Ryan Sapp calling the investigation biased and saying it reached a predetermined conclusion.

cards.headline: Firefighters' union calls St. Lucie County Fire District terminations unjust, disputes hazing findings
cards.teaser: The union representing St. Lucie County Fire District firefighters is demanding arbitration and calling the investigation that led to three terminations and two suspensions biased.
cards.body:
Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County, IAFF Local 1377, said the St. Lucie County Fire District wrongly terminated and suspended five members for their involvement in incidents that occurred in March and September 2024. Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp stated in a letter obtained by WPTV that these incidents did not involve any hazing. Sapp pointed to the Fort Pierce Police Department's report, which he said described the situation, in part, as found coworkers entertaining each other. Local 1377 has demanded arbitration for all five members. The union's position is that all five were wrongly found to be in violation of fire district policies and disciplined without just cause. Sapp also noted that members involved in the incidents were treated differently during the investigative and disciplinary processes, with some receiving no discipline at all.

The union raised concerns about the outside law firm the fire district hired to conduct its investigation, Allen, Norton & Blue. Local 1377 and its legal counsel said the investigation was not conducted in an impartial or unbiased manner. Sapp stated in the letter that the nature of the questions asked, as well as the way in which they were asked or not asked, reflects a predetermined conclusion rather than an objective fact-finding process. Sapp noted that the same firm that conducted the investigation has since been hired by the fire district to represent it at arbitration. The union said it remains willing to negotiate a resolution that would avoid the costs of arbitration and save both the taxpayers and the union a substantial amount of money. Sapp said Fire Chief Jeff Lee has not offered any concessions or proposed resolutions. The St. Lucie County Fire District said it will present the documented facts through the arbitration process and will have no further public comment at this time.

cards.headline: Jealousy over woman led to double fatal shooting in Port St. Lucie, police say
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police said jealousy over a woman prompted an exchange of gunfire early Sunday that killed two Fort Pierce men.
cards.body:
The double fatal shooting occurred at about 3:30 a.m. Sunday in the 1300 block of Southeast Rivergreen Circle. When officers arrived, they found two men with multiple gunshot wounds in the driveways of a residence. Both victims, identified as Carl Loubeau, 24, and Juliun Stokes, 22, both from Fort Pierce, were taken to separate local hospitals, where they later died from their injuries. Police said a verbal altercation occurred outside the residence over a key to a home and escalated into an exchange of gunfire between two of the individuals involved.

Chief Leo Niemczyk said a woman contacted Loubeau, whom she was dating, for a key because she was locked out of her home. When Carl arrived, he found her present with other people, including two males. The motive behind the initial attack was jealousy over the female. Police said Loubeau was the primary aggressor in the dispute, with Dwayne Walker, 20, discharging his firearm in self-defense. Carl approached Juliun and opened fire on him, apparently mistaking Juliun for Dwayne. Dwayne was in close proximity and withdrew his firearm, which is lawfully carried, and started firing on Carl. Niemczyk said their investigation shows that Loubeau fired eight rounds from a 9 mm pistol and one round from a .380 pistol, with Walker firing eight rounds from his .40 caliber pistol. Walker was not injured in the incident. No arrests have been made in the case.

cards.headline: Family files wrongful death lawsuit after 6-year-old dies in go-kart crash at Port St. Lucie Urban Air
cards.teaser: The parents of Emma Riddle allege that Urban Air Trampoline and Adventure Park created dangerous conditions that contributed to their daughter's death in December 2025.
cards.body:
A wrongful death lawsuit was filed Monday against Urban Air Trampoline and Adventure Park in Port St. Lucie after Emma Riddle, 6, was fatally injured at the facility in December 2025. The child's parents allege that Urban Air created dangerous conditions that contributed to Emma's death. Emma visited the adventure park with her mother and sister, where they rode electric go-karts. The child was seated with her mom in a double-seat go-kart while her older sister was in a single-rider go-kart. As outlined in the complaint, there were multiple alleged safety protocols ignored that allegedly led Emma's go-kart to accelerate to a high speed and crash into the track wall, according to the family's attorney, Morgan & Morgan injury law firm. Emma suffered severe injuries and was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died.

Earlier this year, the Florida Department of Agriculture reached a $300,000 settlement agreement with Urban Air Adventure Park following an investigation into the fatal incident. The child's family claims the adventure park ignored safety rules and manufacturer guidelines. At 50 inches, Emma was nearly a foot shorter and twelve years younger than the manufacturer's minimum stated recommendations for operating a double-seat go-kart, and yet, she was permitted to ride, the lawsuit alleges. Morgan & Morgan founder John Morgan said Urban Air has a duty to protect every child that walks through their doors, and alleged that they failed Emma in the most devastating way imaginable.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie couple fights rezoning of lot behind their home, says voices went unheard
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie couple is searching for answers after the city council voted to rezone the lot behind their home from residential to commercial, despite their months-long opposition.
cards.body:
The Mucciolos have called Port St. Lucie home for years, drawn to the property by its beautiful setting and backyard views of nature. In a unanimous vote, the Port St. Lucie City Council approved changing the lot behind their yard, where trees currently stand, to be rezoned from residential to commercial. The council says the change is necessary to reduce traffic in the neighborhood.

 One council member said adding commercial closer to neighborhoods reduces the length of trips, which reduces overall traffic because shorter trips reduce the burden on the overall network. Joseph Mucciolo said the trees will be gone in six months or a year.

 The two spoke at Monday's meeting, voicing their concerns, but they feel the council left them unheard. The council held its second reading Monday. While there was public comment, it was what's called a quasi-judicial hearing, meaning council members act as a panel of judges, applying existing zoning rules to a specific property and making decisions based strictly on sworn testimony and factual evidence, not public opinion.

 Joseph Mucciolo said the couple fought for months and feels their voices have gone unheard except for the news media. The Mucciolos say they will be exploring any kind of appeal process to change this outcome or to change the next one. Margaret Mucciolo said the process needs to change until it's logical, transparent, caring, and provides hope for people.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff ramps up traffic enforcement with focus on speeding, reckless driving
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is intensifying traffic enforcement this summer, deploying additional deputies and launching a new targeting initiative aimed at reducing speeding and reckless driving across the county.
cards.body:
Sheriff Richard Del Toro said traffic is the top concern among residents and described the crackdown as a quality of life issue. Del Toro is using extra deputies from the sheriff's school resource division to boost enforcement while the school year is on break. He is also placing top-performing deputies in areas of concern. Deputies Christopher Rodrigues and Cheyenne Benning are among those targeting high-problem corridors, including Midway Road, U.S. Highway 1 and Indian River Drive.

 Benning said she most recently had someone pass her on I-95 doing 105 mph. Rodrigues said he got a girl doing 72 mph on Midway Road and clocked someone at 98 mph on U.S. Highway 1. On Indian River Drive, which has a 25 mph speed limit, his top speed was 73 mph.

 In the past four weeks, deputies conducted 1,162 traffic stops, wrote 470 citations and issued 1,728 written warnings. The enforcement push is part of a broader strategy Del Toro put in place when he took office. He eliminated the agency's dedicated traffic unit and made traffic enforcement the responsibility of every deputy. Since 2025, the sheriff's office has issued more than 26,000 citations, a 155% increase.

hero.headline: Fellsmere animal sanctuary rebuilds with $100,000 in community support after fire killed 11 cats
hero.body:
A Fellsmere animal sanctuary is rebuilding with more than $100,000 in community support after a fire on March 9 destroyed the facility and killed 11 cats. Ted Pankiewicz, founder of For the Love of Paws, suffered burns to his arms during the fire as he tried to save the animals. He started the nonprofit sanctuary in 2014 in memory of his late wife, who had always dreamed of starting a rescue. The sanctuary now serves some of the Treasure Coast's most vulnerable residents by supplying 12,000 to 15,000 pounds of pet food each month to senior citizens, disabled people, and veterans who are struggling to feed their pets.

For the Love of Paws operates as a sanctuary rather than a traditional rescue, which means animals that arrive stay for the rest of their lives. "We are a sanctuary, we're not a rescue… when your pets come here, they come here for the rest of their life. We take care of them as our very own," Pankiewicz said. The facility provides permanent homes for animals in a cage-free environment where they are treated as family members.

The new facility will be constructed entirely of steel and will include enhanced safety features designed to prevent another tragedy. A security system will be installed that alerts the fire department directly when smoke is detected. An interior sprinkler system will also be added throughout the building. "The new building is going to be all steel… and we're going to be having a security system put in where the smoke detectors immediately alert the fire department, and there will be a sprinkler system inside too… which I'm sure will piss off the cats, but it's better," Pankiewicz said.

The community response to the tragedy deeply moved Pankiewicz, who struggled to find adequate words to express his gratitude. "The response from the community was just as emotional as the fire was, but in the opposite… the fire made us cry tears of sorrow, and the community made us cry tears of gratitude," Pankiewicz said. The funds raised will cover the cost of the new construction and safety systems. The rebuilt sanctuary is expected to feature a cage-free space with an outdoor catio where cats can roam freely, continuing the mission that Pankiewicz began in honor of his wife's dream.

cards.headline: JetBlue ending Vero Beach to New York JFK route in September due to low demand

cards.body:
JetBlue is canceling its flight route between Vero Beach Regional Airport and New York's JFK Airport, with the last flights operating in September. The airline cited low demand as the reason for ending the route, which launched last December to excitement from Treasure Coast residents hoping for convenient travel options to the Northeast. Brandon Dambeck, interim airport director, said the decision reflects how the airline industry operates based on passenger numbers.

 "It's just the way that that market works, and air carriers will fluctuate based off of demand," Dambeck said. He added that JetBlue "just wasn't seeing what they were hoping for" with the New York route.

 Not everyone agrees the route had a fair shot at success. Charlie Ahern, who regularly uses JetBlue flights at Vero Beach Regional Airport, said he believes the route would have grown over time if given more opportunity. "I think if they hung in there, it would have worked.

 I think it would have built up pretty good," Ahern said. He noted the convenience of flying out of Vero Beach, saying, "It's easy. It's close." His comments reflect concerns from local travelers who appreciated having direct access to New York without driving to larger airports in South Florida or Orlando.

 The Boston route continues to perform well at Vero Beach Regional Airport, with Dambeck saying "Boston is seeing great demand." Grece Ezzi flew into Vero Beach on JetBlue from Boston on Friday for the first time, demonstrating continued interest in that northeastern connection. The contrast between the two routes highlights how different markets can perform differently even when serving similar geographic regions. While both Boston and New York are major northeastern cities, the Boston service has attracted enough passengers to remain viable while the JFK route struggled to build a sustainable customer base.

 Dambeck said the door is not closed on the JFK route returning in the future, noting "They'll evaluate continuously. So just because it's gone now doesn't mean that it never will come back." This leaves open the possibility that JetBlue could restore service to New York if conditions change or demand increases. Airlines regularly reassess their route networks based on seasonal patterns, economic conditions, and shifting travel preferences. For now, Vero Beach travelers seeking to reach New York will need to connect through other cities or use alternative airports.

cards.headline: Indian River County families can apply for free or reduced-price student meals starting July 15
cards.teaser: Families in Indian River County are able to apply for free or reduced price meals for students starting July 15.
cards.body:
Families in Indian River County can apply for free or reduced-price meals for students starting July 15 through the district's online portal. While six schools in the county will automatically provide free meals to all students during the 2026-2027 school year through federal nutrition programs, other families may still qualify based on household size and income levels.

 The application process begins at www.LINQConnect.com, where parents must either sign in to an existing account or create a new one. After logging in, families should search for Indian River County Public Schools in Vero Beach and add their student to the application using the Student ID number and the child's formal name as it appears in FOCUS, the district's student information system. The application can be accessed from the website homepage by clicking School Services at the top menu and then selecting Free and Reduced Meal Application.

 District officials are encouraging families to submit one application per household to determine eligibility. The application requires families to provide information about household size and income to determine eligibility for the federal nutrition programs. By submitting a single application for all children in the household, families can streamline the process and find out if they qualify for free meals, reduced-price meals, or neither option. The program is designed to ensure that students have access to nutritious meals during the school day regardless of their family's financial situation.

 Families who have questions about the meal programs or need assistance with the application process can contact Shawn O'Keefe, the district's nutrition services director. O'Keefe can be reached by phone at (772) 564-5041 or by email at shawn.okeefe@indianriverschools.org. District officials recommend that families apply as early as possible to ensure their eligibility status is determined before the start of the 2026-2027 school year.

cards.headline: JetBlue ending direct flights from Vero Beach to JFK Airport in September
cards.teaser: JetBlue is ending its direct flights between New York's JFK Airport and Vero Beach Regional Airport, citing low passenger demand for the route that launched in December.
cards.body:
JetBlue is ending its direct flights between New York's JFK Airport and Vero Beach Regional Airport, citing low passenger demand for the route that launched in December. The airline announced that service between the two airports will end Sept. 9, just nine months after the route began operating with much fanfare and optimistic passengers. JetBlue said in a statement that demand for this new route has not materialized as the airline had hoped. JetBlue will continue serving Vero Beach through its Boston route and has not announced whether it plans to add any replacement routes from Vero Beach or if it will adjust frequency on the remaining Boston service.

 All affected customers will be notified directly by JetBlue and will receive full refunds. Passengers with upcoming reservations on the discontinued route are encouraged to contact JetBlue directly or check their email for rebooking options and refund information. The JFK-Vero Beach route was seen as a major win for the Treasure Coast when it launched in December 2025, providing direct access to one of the nation's busiest airports and potentially boosting tourism to the area. The inaugural flight brought enthusiastic passengers who called the service a game changer for connecting family and friends between New York and the Treasure Coast.

 The route's cancellation comes as a disappointment to local officials and residents who had hoped the direct connection would strengthen ties between the two regions. The discontinuation of the JFK route after such a short period highlights the challenges smaller regional airports face in sustaining air service to major hubs. While JetBlue's Boston service will continue to provide some connectivity for Vero Beach travelers, the loss of direct access to JFK eliminates what many saw as a crucial link to the New York metropolitan area. The airline has not indicated whether it might reconsider the route in the future or explore other destinations from Vero Beach Regional Airport.

 The route had been viewed as important infrastructure for the region when it first began operations, with hopes that convenient access to JFK would help strengthen economic and personal connections between the Treasure Coast and the New York metropolitan area. The short lifespan of the route underscores the difficulties regional airports encounter when trying to establish and maintain service to major transportation hubs.

cards.headline: Vero Beach parents sue city over infant son's remains allegedly disturbed and reburied without consent
cards.teaser: Adam Chrzan and Tanya Crovo allege their infant son's remains were disturbed during maintenance at Crestlawn Cemetery and reinterred without their knowledge.
cards.body:
Adam Chrzan and Tanya Crovo have filed an amended lawsuit against the City of Vero Beach alleging their infant son's remains were disturbed during maintenance work at Crestlawn Cemetery and reburied without their knowledge or consent. The couple's son, identified in court documents only as A.C., died in August 2007 at 37 days old and was buried at the city-owned cemetery. The parents say they did not learn about what allegedly happened until April 2025, nearly 18 years after their son's burial.

 According to the complaint, sometime between the 2007 burial and April 2025, heavy equipment being used for maintenance or irrigation work near the burial site breached the grave, damaging or destroying the casket, its contents, and the child's remains. The lawsuit alleges that someone acting in an official capacity for the City of Vero Beach then directed cemetery workers to collect the remains, place them into a new casket, and reinter the child without notifying the parents or obtaining their consent. The amended complaint accuses the city and cemetery of tortious interference with a burial plot and human remains, negligence, negligent infliction of emotional distress, intentional misrepresentation, and fraudulent concealment.

 This amended complaint comes after a judge dismissed the family's original lawsuit. The dismissal was not a finding that the allegations were false but rather a ruling that the legal claims as originally pleaded could not proceed against the city under Florida law. The parents have now refiled with different legal arguments in an attempt to overcome the previous dismissal. A judge has not yet ruled on the amended complaint. The City of Vero Beach has declined to comment on the amended complaint.

 In court filings responding to the original lawsuit, the city disputed the allegation that irrigation work could have caused the damage described by the parents. The city submitted a survey stating there are no irrigation lines adjacent to the burial plot of A.C. The case highlights the legal protections cities have under Florida law and the challenges families face when seeking accountability for alleged mishandling of cemetery operations. The amended complaint represents the parents' continued effort to hold the city responsible for what they describe as the unauthorized disturbance and reburial of their infant son's remains.
